sections.title: ① Concept Explanation
sections.body:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a hybrid AI architecture that combines a **retrieval system** (which fetches relevant documents from a knowledge base) with a **generative language model** (which synthesizes the retrieved content into a coherent answer). Introduced by Lewis et al. (2020) at Meta, RAG addresses the core limitations of pure LLMs: static parametric knowledge, hallucination, and inability to cite sources. In production, RAG acts as a dynamic memory layer — the retriever queries a vector database or search index at inference time, retrieves the top-K most relevant chunks, and injects them into the LLM prompt as grounding context. This enables the LLM to answer questions about documents it was never trained on, provide up-to-date information without retraining, and attribute claims to specific source documents.

**Architecture Overview:**
```
User Query → Query Encoder → Vector DB Retrieval → Context Injection → LLM → Answer
                ↑                    ↑
         Embedding Model      Indexed Document Store
```

diagrams.title: RAG = an offline indexing pipeline + an online query pipeline
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  subgraph OFF["Offline — indexing (runs when documents change)"]
    direction TB
    D["Documents"] --> L["Load + parse"] --> C["Chunk"] --> E1["Embed chunks"] --> V[("Vector index + metadata")]
  end
  subgraph ON["Online — every question"]
    direction TB
    Q["User question"] --> E2["Embed query"] --> R["Retrieve top-k"] --> P["Prompt = instructions + chunks + question"] --> G["LLM generates grounded answer"]
  end
  V -. "similarity search" .-> R
diagrams.explain: RAG has **two pipelines**. The offline one turns documents into searchable chunks and runs only when content changes. The online one runs for every question: embed the query, fetch the most similar chunks, and put them in the prompt so the model answers from *your* data instead of its memory. Most RAG bugs live in the offline half (bad parsing, bad chunks), even though they show up as bad answers.

quiz.question: What problem does RAG fundamentally solve that fine-tuning cannot?
options: Advanced RAG improves a fixed pipeline; Modular RAG decouples the pipeline into composable modules with defined interfaces.
RAG natively supports per-user retrieval filtering (metadata filters on vector DB).
In bi-encoder RAG, the query encoder and document encoder are typically the same model (e.g., text-embedding-3-large), because they must produce vectors in the same…
Fine-tuning bakes knowledge into model weights — it's static, expensive to update, and doesn't provide citations.
quiz.explanation: Fine-tuning bakes knowledge into model weights — it's static, expensive to update, and doesn't provide citations. RAG externalizes knowledge into a retrieval store that can be updated independently of the model.

quiz.question: Explain the three phases of a RAG pipeline: indexing, retrieval, and generation.
options: Prompt stuffing: $500-5,000/month (token costs). Fine-tuning: $10,000-50,000 training cost amortized + inference.
Unoptimized pipeline with synchronous blocking calls and no caching.
Yes — this is the production gold standard called RAG + RAFT (Retrieval-Augmented Fine-Tuning).
Indexing (offline): Documents are loaded, chunked, embedded via an embedding model, and stored in a vector database with metadata.
quiz.explanation: Indexing (offline): Documents are loaded, chunked, embedded via an embedding model, and stored in a vector database with metadata. This is a batch process. Retrieval (online): The user's query is embedded using the same model, and a similarity search (ANN) retrieves the top-K most relevant chunks.

quiz.question: What is the difference between the query encoder and document encoder in RAG, and must they be the same model?
options: Implement async FastAPI server with connection pooling to vector DB and LLM.
Users phrase queries colloquially ("what's the return window?") while documents use formal language ("merchandise returns are accepted within 30 calendar days").
Prompt stuffing (also called "context stuffing") inserts all relevant documents directly into the LLM's context window without any retrieval step.
In bi-encoder RAG, the query encoder and document encoder are typically the same model (e.g., text-embedding-3-large), because they must produce vectors in the same…
quiz.explanation: In bi-encoder RAG, the query encoder and document encoder are typically the same model (e.g., text-embedding-3-large), because they must produce vectors in the same embedding space for similarity comparison to be meaningful. However, asymmetric models like BAAI/bge-large-en-v1.5 use instruction prefixes — queries get "Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: " while documents get no prefix.

quiz.question: What are the latency components in a RAG pipeline and how do you profile them?
options: Long-context LLMs can theoretically accept entire document corpora in-context, but have critical limitations at scale: (a) cost — 1M tokens per query costs ~$3-7 per…
Advanced RAG improves a fixed pipeline; Modular RAG decouples the pipeline into composable modules with defined interfaces.
Stale index — new clinical guidelines were published but the index was never updated.
RAG latency breaks down into: (1) query embedding (~10-50ms for API, ~5ms local), (2) vector DB retrieval (~5-50ms for HNSW at scale), (3) optional reranking…
quiz.explanation: RAG latency breaks down into: (1) query embedding (~10-50ms for API, ~5ms local), (2) vector DB retrieval (~5-50ms for HNSW at scale), (3) optional reranking (~100-500ms), (4) LLM generation (~500ms-5s). Total wall-clock time is typically 700ms-6s. Profile each stage independently. ---

quiz.question: How does RAG handle knowledge that changes frequently (e.g., daily news, live stock prices)?
options: Distribution shift between test and production queries. Test queries were curated; production queries are messier.
Yes — this is the production gold standard called RAG + RAFT (Retrieval-Augmented Fine-Tuning).
Prompt stuffing: $500-5,000/month (token costs). Fine-tuning: $10,000-50,000 training cost amortized + inference.
RAG handles dynamic knowledge via incremental index updates: when new documents arrive, they're chunked, embedded, and upserted to the vector store without rebuilding…
quiz.explanation: RAG handles dynamic knowledge via incremental index updates: when new documents arrive, they're chunked, embedded, and upserted to the vector store without rebuilding the entire index. For truly real-time data (stock prices, live metrics), RAG is often combined with tool use — the LLM calls a live API rather than retrieving from a static store.
